_README: THE PUBLICATION MANIFEST (D-031): the only list of repository documents that may reach a public surface (the docs site).
A page is published only if tools/publish/core.py's publishable_guard accepts its src: the file exists, is Markdown, is not under never_publish, is not a file C3 skips by name

(a path ending in psyche_roadmap.md or DECISIONS.md), sits outside every directory ledger_check skips (SKIP_DIRS and every hidden directory), is in neither claim_quarantine_paths nor count_quarantine_paths of tools/ledger.json,
carries no ledger ignore-file pragma, is in the tree of the commit being published and does not differ from that commit on disk.
So only text that ledger_check's C2, C3 and C4 actually govern, as a commit holds it, can be published. Adding a page here never bypasses the guard.
slug is the site route below site_base; wiki is a leftover page name from the wiki that is no longer built, and is not published. Relative links to these sources are rewritten to those targets;
links to any other tracked file become GitHub links pinned to the publishing commit, and a dead relative link fails the build.
never_publish entries ending in / are directory prefixes; the others are files. Each must be a canonical relative path (no leading / or ./, no backslash), or the manifest is refused.
Matching is case-insensitive, so it can only refuse more, never less. tools/publish/render_plan.py also renders generated blocks in the pages listed here.

title, where given, replaces a page's first heading as its site title. description is the page's meta description and its link preview: one plain sentence of 120 to 160 characters that no other page repeats, written from the page itself with no figure typed by hand. tools/publish/stage.py writes it into the staged page and refuses a page that has none.

pages.description: A guide to Psyche, an open research project that builds brain-inspired components in stages, with AGI as its long-term aim, and to where each reader goes next.
Answers to common questions about Psyche: why AGI is named as its long-term aim, why some work stays private, whether it uses a language model, and who runs it.
The public record of Psyche's research plan: phases started and finished, gates decided, dates changed and commitments made, with an Atom feed to follow it.
How Psyche is run: who leads it, the four roles that keep its evidence honest, what happens if the work stops, its funding, and a note on ethics and safety.
Overview of stage 2 of Psyche: a test of whether a spiking network with local plasticity shows, on classic tests, behaviour that an internal map would explain.
How the substrate, stage 1 of Psyche, led to stage 2: what it built and showed, what carries into spiking cognitive maps, and where the stages point.
The phases of stage 2 of Psyche, the layers that keep the line standing if the main goal falls short, and the paper deadline, with dates read from the plan.
The decision gates of stage 2 of Psyche: the question each gate asks, the fallback if it is missed and its public status, with dates read from the plan.
The classic animal-learning paradigms behind the stage 2 test battery, what each one probes, and the rules that keep every agent on the same footing.
What stage 2 of Psyche may say about its model, what the line covers, and how a new idea is kept out of it: the rules for every public sentence.
The engineering standards of stage 2 of Psyche: how its code is written and its analysis is done, so that every number the line reports can be traced.
Definitions of the terms used on the cognitive-map pages and in the substrate record, grouped by topic, each explained as these pages use it.
The classic works behind the question of stage 2: behaviour that suggests animals learn maps, the neural findings tied to it, and the limits on energy claims.
The public summary of the release rule for stage 2 of Psyche: what is public now, what is withheld, and the conditions under which material is released.

pages.title: The substrate
pages.description: The substrate, stage 1 of Psyche: a dependency-free Python memory-and-activation prototype, what is verified, what is not claimed, and where it stands.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.description: The as-built reference for the substrate's code: its modules, data model, public surfaces and invariants, and the reasons behind the key design decisions.

pages.title: Methodology
pages.description: How test-first, adversarial development of the substrate caught structural bugs, each traceable to the code and tests, and where it drew the line on claims.
The substrate's three negative results: why priming, the fan effect and interoception each stopped before a graded run, and what that pattern shows.
